lesson.title: One Line, Anchored at the Center of the Data
lesson.summary: The regression line is the geometric picture of the least squares slope and intercept, a single straight line, always passing through the mean point, that can be drawn directly on the scatterplot.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter produced two numbers, a slope and an intercept, chosen because together they minimize the sum of squared residuals. This chapter is about the resulting object as a geometric fact rather than a formula: a single straight line that can be drawn directly across the scatterplot and read like any other line on a graph.

One property of this line is guaranteed by the way its intercept was built: it always passes through the point formed by the mean of x and the mean of y, sometimes called the balance point of the data. For the hours studied example, that point is 3 hours and 69 points. Plugging x equal to 3 into the line, predicted score equals 39 plus 10 times 3, which is 39 plus 30, equal to 69, exactly the mean score. This is not a coincidence specific to this one data set, it is a direct consequence of how the intercept formula, mean of y minus slope times mean of x, was derived, and it holds for every least squares line ever fit to any data.

It is worth being precise about what the regression line is not. It does not connect the data points in order, and it is not required to pass through any individual observation at all. In the five student example, the line passes near several points but does not land exactly on most of them, since it was built to minimize overall squared distance across all five points at once, not to touch any particular one of them. It is a mathematical summary of the trend running through the cloud, not a connect the dots picture of the actual data.

This objectivity is also what separates the regression line from a line drawn by eye. Two students sketching a best fit line through the same scatterplot by hand will often draw visibly different lines, since eyeballing depends on individual judgment about where a line looks centered. The least squares line, by contrast, is completely determined by the data through the minimization rule, so anyone who computes it correctly from the same data set gets the identical line every single time, with no room for disagreement.

In practice, drawing this line on a scatterplot takes only two points, since any two points determine a unique straight line. Using the equation from the previous chapter, at 1 hour studied the line sits at 39 plus 10 times 1, equal to 49, and at 5 hours studied it sits at 39 plus 10 times 5, equal to 89. Plotting the points (1, 49) and (5, 89) and connecting them with a straightedge reproduces the exact same least squares line described algebraically, stretching cleanly across the full range of the observed data.

Finally, the regression line is only trustworthy when the scatterplot's form is actually linear to begin with. Fitting a straight line through the earlier U-shaped example, where y was determined by the squared distance of x from 3, would produce a flat, nearly horizontal line that misses the real pattern entirely, since the least squares method assumes a straight line shape is a reasonable target in the first place. Checking the form on the scatterplot always comes before trusting any line drawn through it, no matter how the slope and intercept were calculated.
